rate.text: Families were assigned by chance, and the gap was big and pointed the same way in every trial. But families and therapists knew who got what, and two of the four small trials came from a team including CRAFT's developer.
rate.reason: The rating was lowered one level for how the trials were run (risk of bias), not for their size or US setting: imprecision and indirectness were not rated down, so 'only four small US trials' points at the wrong reasons, and the first named reason (families and therapists knew the assignment) was missing. 'CRAFT's creators' overstates 'a team that includes CRAFT's developer'.

item.statement: Indica and sativa labels tell you which smell compounds your weed has.
item.why: In 41,201 US lab-tested samples, the labels barely matched the mix of smell compounds (terpenes). The labels came from a strain website, not the bags, and effects weren't measured.

quiz.reason: Supported, one fact, worth telling. Wording only: 'a weed has' reads like a garden weed; the why said 'terpene mix' where the statement says 'smell compounds' (one word for one thing); 'not the bags' carries the but line's limit.

Certainty beyond the lines: a general rule about sativa and indica strains is answered false from one small study of two strains (the why itself says 'not a rule'), and the lines give no THC comparison between labels in the large US data. Scoped to that one study it would be too narrow to be worth a reader's time.

item.statement: Benzo withdrawal can feel like the anxiety or sleep problems the pills were for.
item.why: The reviews say withdrawal symptoms can feel like the original problem. They're expert reviews, not studies, so this is second-hand.

quiz.reason: Useful, supported and kept second-hand. Only change: the lines do not say that both reviews make this point (how point 2 leaves it unattributed), so 'Both' is dropped; 'not studies' as in the but line.

item.statement: Two expert reviews that warn of seizures after stopping benzos suddenly say how often they happen.
item.why: Both warn the seizures can be life-threatening, but neither gives a rate. The only count they give is 2 of 11 prisoners in 1961, in conditions unlike usual use.

quiz.reason: 'Reviews that warn...' answered false generalizes beyond the two reviews the lines describe, so the statement is scoped to them; 'Both reviews read warn' was garbled. The why now opens with the danger (how point 3: life-threatening) so the missing rate cannot read as reassurance about stopping suddenly, and the 1961 count is marked as the reviews' own.

fields.but: The labels came from a strain website, not the bags. And nobody measured how the weed made people feel.
how: Researchers used lab results for about 90,000 flower samples from licensed growers in six US states, 2013 to 2021. Labels came from a strain website, matched by name. They didn't check whether the labels differed in THC or CBD.

In 41,201 samples where THC outweighed CBD, the three labels were all mixed up in their terpenes. Sativa was twice as common in one smell type, rich in terpinolene, but most of those were still hybrid.
Strain names did better: for 26 of 41 widely grown names, different growers' products were more alike than chance. For 13 they weren't, and two, LSD and Durban Poison, were less alike.
A small Dutch study tested two coffee-shop strains, one sativa-type and one indica-type. They had similar THC but different terpenes, and each varied a lot from bag to bag.

lines.reason: q asks 'what's in your weed' and short answers 'Mostly not', but THC and CBD were not compared between the labels (statement), so a reader could take the answer as covering THC; how point 1 now says so. How point 2: 'THC-dominant' is the balance of THC to CBD, not a high THC level. but: 'how the weed felt' can read as its texture. q, short and how points 3 and 4 are fine.

fields.short: Family skills training called CRAFT worked best in trials. In one, 64 in 100 relatives who'd refused help started treatment, against 30 with confrontation training and 13 with counselling to join Al-Anon.
fields.but: Just four small US trials, and two came from a team that includes CRAFT's developer.
how: The biggest trial had 130 family members, mostly women, living with someone with a drinking problem. Each got one of three approaches by chance. Families with recent or severe violence were left out.

Within 6 months, 64 in 100 relatives started treatment after CRAFT. It was 30 after training for a family confrontation, and 13 after counselling to join Al-Anon. Seven in 10 families chose not to hold the confrontation.
Across four trials, two about alcohol and two about other drugs, 67 in 100 relatives started treatment with CRAFT, against 18 in 100 with Al-Anon or Nar-Anon approaches: about 3 times as often.

In the biggest trial, family members felt less depressed and angry after 6 months in every group, whether or not their relative started treatment. Every group got some help, so no approach can take the credit.

lines.reason: short: names the two comparisons, since a reader weighing a family confrontation needs to know it did worse (the 6-month window stays in how point 2). but: the statement says 'a team that includes CRAFT's developer', not the team that created it. How point 1: 'about 12 hours each' is given only for CRAFT, not the other two approaches; and the exclusion of families with recent or severe violence, a safety limit, was in no line. How point 3: absolute numbers before relative ones. How point 4: the wellbeing result is from the biggest trial only, not the four pooled; plainer last sentence.

fields.short: It can be: two expert reviews warn of life-threatening seizures, but not how often. The only count they give is 2 of 11 prisoners on very high doses, in 1961.
fields.but: These are expert reviews, not studies. Their seizure warnings give no rates, and one gives no source for them.
how: One review says withdrawal symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use, in about 15 to 30 in 100 people. That figure comes from the author's own earlier paper.

Symptoms listed include anxiety, poor sleep, aches, tingling and sensitivity to light and sound, and can feel like the problem the pills were for. Sleeping pills stopped after even a few nights can bring back worse sleep for a while.

Both warn that seizures after stopping suddenly can be life-threatening. One says severe reactions can also happen when cutting down slowly, and that many reports are anecdotes; the other gives no source for its warning.
The only count comes second-hand, from a 1961 study: 11 prisoners who had taken very high doses for months were switched to a dummy pill. Ten had withdrawal, and 2 had seizures.

lines.reason: The 1961 count is known only through the reviews (the study was not read), so short and how point 4 now say it is second-hand. but: the 2015 review cites the 2011 one elsewhere, so 'no source at all' overstates; it gives none for its seizure warnings. How point 2: rebound comes on stopping and lasts 'for a while' (statement); as written it could read as the pills themselves worsening sleep. How point 3: the statement says 'many' severe reactions are reported anecdotally, not 'most'; 'tapering' in plain words. q and how point 1 are fine; nothing reads as advice on how to stop.

how: 2,115 Australian festival-goers, most of whom had used drugs, volunteered for an online survey. Each read about a made-up festival with no police, and one with police, riot police, sniffer dogs or police working with health services.
With any police, 70 in 100 said they'd use drugs and 53 in 100 that they'd carry drugs in, against 77 and 63 with no police. With sniffer dogs, 47 in 100 said they'd carry drugs in.
Slightly more said they'd buy drugs inside the festival when police were there: 40 against 37 in 100. The authors worry those drugs may not be what they're sold as, which wasn't checked.
Police working with health services made almost no difference: 75 in 100 still said they'd use drugs. The study says nothing about how much people would take.

lines.reason: How point 4: amounts were collected but not analysed (statement), so 'the survey didn't ask' is wrong. How point 1: the sample chose to take part, so its figures describe it, not festival-goers in general (statement); 'health services' in both places for the same thing. q, short and but are fine: every figure stays a stated intention about a made-up festival, and nothing reads as how to get past police or dogs.
